strengths: Genuine methodological novelty: combining invisible-Unicode watermarking with a cue/reply split and a ranking test against reserved counterfactual watermarks yields a text-preserving auditing method with a provable FPR bound (FPR ≤ k/K), addressing a real gap versus visible 'copyright traps' and unreliable MIAs.
Clear and well-motivated problem framing, including a thoughtful discussion of the legal context (EU AI Act, ongoing US litigation) that grounds the practical relevance of the work.

The requirements-driven design (text authenticity, scalability, robustness, black-box operability, soundness, completeness) is clearly mapped onto concrete construction choices (syllable/cue/reply structure, cross-bifix-free-like constraints, TTP-issued candidate sets).

Reasonably thorough multi-axis empirical evaluation (collection size, training-set size, number of concurrent watermarks, ranking-based decision test) across two model families and two text domains, with informative per-chunk hit-probability estimates (p, p_FN).

Honest and fairly detailed limitations section covering robustness to normalization/adversarial removal, reliance on a trusted third party, and scope restricted to LoRA fine-tuning, without overselling generality.
Reasonable reproducibility support: open-weight models, explicit hyperparameters/appendix details, and a stated intent to release code and evaluation scripts.
weaknesses: No empirical robustness evaluation against the most obvious and trivial attack: stripping/filtering zero-width Unicode characters, which any moderately aware data curator or platform could apply, would fully defeat the scheme; this is only discussed qualitatively as future work despite being central to real-world viability.

The method requires marking documents prospectively, before any potential misuse; it cannot help authors/rightsholders audit content that has already been published and potentially scraped, which is arguably the dominant real-world use case motivating the paper's legal framing (e.g., existing books/news already used in training).

Evaluation is limited to two 7B open-weight models fine-tuned via LoRA on modest-scale data (≤15k documents); no experiments with larger models, full fine-tuning, RLHF, closed-weight APIs, or realistically sized commercial fine-tuning corpora, which limits confidence that results generalize to the settings the paper motivates (bank chatbots, GPT-scale systems).

Claimed scalability of the watermark space (millions of watermarks) is only a theoretical combinatorial argument; the actual multi-watermark experiments test at most 12 concurrent watermarks and K=100 candidate sets, far short of validating claims about large-scale multi-user deployment or collision behavior at scale.

Limited statistical rigor: most results are averaged over only 5 runs with reported standard deviations but no significance testing, and some described trends (e.g., Poems dataset regurgitation dropping from 28 to 26 as dataset size quadruples) are used to support robustness claims despite being a fairly small, noisy effect.

No direct experimental comparison against the closest existing text-preserving alternative (homoglyph-based watermarks of Wei et al.), leaving the claimed advantages (e.g., degradation with more watermarks) only qualitatively argued rather than empirically demonstrated head-to-head.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with some inconsistencies (e.g., overloaded symbol λ used both as the verification repetition count and, apparently, as a step variable in Algorithm 1's mark procedure), which could hinder reproducibility and comprehension.

Ethical treatment of embedding invisible marks into third-party personal data (e.g., blogs, CVs) without the data subject's consent is acknowledged but not deeply resolved; the paper's own stated goal of empowering individuals to protect their data sits in tension with a technique that itself modifies personal documents' byte-level content without consent frameworks in place.
